newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr off highs in late Tokyo, capped by exporters.
newsitem.headline: Dlr off highs in late Tokyo, capped by exporters.

text.p: 0630 GMT TRADED HIGH/LOW AS OF 0600 GMT

The dollar was off its highs against the yen by late afternoon Tokyo on Friday, but found indirect support from short-covering interest in mark/yen after the Bundesbank chief said overnight the dollar's recovery from historic lows in 1995 had come to an end.
"Short-covering interest in mark/yen was very strong after (Hans) Tietmeyer's remarks," said a trust bank trader.
Tietmeyer said on Thursday he believed that the dollar's correction has clearly come to an end.
Tietmeyer also said that the German central bank was closely watching developments on forex markets and was determined that the mark would remain strong in the run-up to the euro launch in 1999.
The mark stood at 64.96/99 yen as of 0645 GMT, up from around 64.60 yen in late Thursday in New York.
In Thursday's Tokyo trade, the mark/yen fell to a near two-year low of 63.74 yen.
The greenback briefly touched 114 yen in early afternoon trade, as stop-losses were triggered at around 113.50, 113.70 and 113.80 yen, a trader at another trust bank said.
However, interbank players quickly took profits as the dollar's rise was capped by exporter offers above 114 yen.
The market could still try to push the dollar/yen higher over the next few days, as it has confirmed that support for the dollar is solid near 112 yen, a city bank trader said.
"Japanese authorities have shown their determination to check the dollar's slide. Japanese institutional investors are also expected to bid the dollar near 112 yen," he said.

Makoto Utsumi, former MOF vice minister of international affairs, said in an interview with a Japanese economic daily that financial authorities in the U.S. and Japan could step in or intervene verbally if the yen appreciates beyond 110 yen.

"If the yen advances past 110 yen to the dollar, Japanese and U.S. authorities are likely to send a signal to the market," Utsumi was quoted as saying in Friday's edition of the Nikkei Financial Daily.
The article gave another reminder to the market that MOF would prevent the dollar from falling below 110 yen, a trader at another city bank said.
The U.S. producer price index (PPI) for June, due at 1230 GMT, is unlikely to have a strong impact on the forex market unless it sharply deviates from expectations, traders said.
The average forecast of economists polled by Reuters indicated the PPI would be unchanged from the previous month.

"Prices have been stable in the United States. Unless a surprisingly high or low figure moves U.S. stock and bond markets, the PPI data is unlikely to move the forex market," said a trust bank trader.
Operators may be more interested in the Bank of Japan's branch managers' meeting which starts on Monday, he said.

The Philippine Central Bank said it would allow the peso to move in a wider range versus the dollar. However, this did not trigger similar safe-haven yen buying as was seen last week after Thailand announced it would float the baht, traders said.

A Singapore bank dealer said the dollar/mark looked set to weaken as it would be difficult to ignore the strong signals sent by the Bundesbank overnight, although Germany's fundamentals remained relatively unattractive.
The dollar closed at 113.12/17 yen and 1.7513/18 marks in New York on Thursday. -- Singapore newsroom (65-8703080)
-- Kanta Watanabe, Tokyo Treasury Desk +81-3-3432-9780
